Patients with heart failure are vulnerable to the SARS-CoV-2 infection.
However, limited evidence exists on the safety of the SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccines in this patient population.

The objective of this study was to investigate the risk of all-cause mortality, worsening heart failure, venous thromboembolism, and myocarditis associated with the mRNA vaccines in patients with heart failure.

Using Danish nationwide registries, 2 cohorts were constructed: (1) all prevalent heart failure patients in 2019 aged 40 to 95 years and (2) all prevalent heart failure patients in 2021 aged 40 to 95 years, who were vaccinated with either of the 2 mRNA vaccines (BNT162B2 or mRNA-1273).
The patients in the 2 cohorts were matched 1:1 using exact exposure matching on age, sex, and duration of heart failure.
To estimate standardized absolute risks, outcome-specific Cox regression analyses were performed.
The total study population comprised 101 786 patients.
The median age of the study population was 74 years (interquartile range, 66–81).

The standardized risk of all-cause mortality within 90 days was 2.23% (95% CI, 2.10%–2.36%) in the vaccinated cohort and 2.56% (95% CI, 2.43%–2.70%) in the unvaccinated cohort (90-day risk difference, −0.33% [95% CI, −0.52% to −0.15%]).

The standardized risk of worsening heart failure within 90 days was 1.10% (95% CI, −1.01% to 1.19%) in the 2021 (vaccinated) cohort and 1.08% (95% CI, 0.99%–1.17%) in the 2019 (unvaccinated) cohort (risk difference, 0.02% [95% CI, −0.11% to 0.15%]).
No significant differences were found regarding venous thromboembolism or myocarditis.
Receiving an mRNA vaccine was not associated with an increased risk of worsening heart failure, myocarditis, venous thromboembolism, or all-cause mortality.
WHAT IS NEW?
This study provides insight into the safety of the SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccines when used in patients of heart failure.

Analyzing over 100 000 patients with heart failure, no safety concerns were found regarding the risk of all-cause mortality, worsening heart failure, myocarditis, or venous thromboembolism in patients with heart failure vaccinated with any of the SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccines.
WHAT ARE THE CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS?
This study emphasizes the safety of the mRNA vaccines in patients with heart failure.
The use of COVID-19 vaccines will continue to be important in preventing morbidity and mortality in vulnerable patient populations, such as patients with heart failure.
Thus, studies emphasizing the safety of the vaccines are empirical to secure a continued uptake of COVID-19 vaccines and prevent concerns in those that might hesitate to take the vaccine.

Risk factors for serious disease with the SARS-CoV-2 include preexisting cardiovascular disease, and especially patients with heart failure constitute a population at a high risk of hospitalization, morbidity, and mortality.1 In the absence of effective treatment, vaccines are the best prevention for morbidity and mortality in patients with heart failure, and for this reason, vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 is highly recommended in this patient population.1,2 Recent studies have shown that vaccination in patients with heart failure significantly reduces the risk of all-cause mortality and risk of hospital admission, compared with not vaccinating in patients with heart failure.3 However, little is still known about the safety of the mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccines in patients with heart failure.1 Some concerns remain regarding the safety of the mRNA vaccines in patients with heart failure, especially in relation to a perceived higher risk of cardiovascular side effects such as myocarditis.1 All of the vaccine trials included patients with stable cardiovascular disease.

However, these studies included only a limited number of patients with heart failure, and no separate analyses were performed regarding the safety of the vaccines in this subgroup of patients.4–6 Large real-world studies have been performed; however, these studies also did not specifically examine patients with cardiovascular disease.2,6–9 Thus, there is a need for a real-world safety study, with the focus on this specific subpopulation of patients who are especially vulnerable to SARS-CoV-2 infection, and that may also be at a higher risk of cardiovascular side effects from the mRNA vaccines.1 The aims of this study are, therefore, to investigate the risk of all-cause mortality, worsening heart failure, venous thromboembolism, and myocarditis associated with the mRNA vaccines in patients with heart failure.

Data underlying the study cannot be made publicly available, as access to Danish Registry Data must be granted to researchers or institutions on an individual basis by the Danish Data Protection Agency.

Based on _International Classification of Diseases_,_Tenth Revision_, diagnoses codes for heart failure, prevalent heart failure patients were identified and defined as patients with existing heart failure.

Two cohorts were constructed: (1) with all prevalent heart failure patients in 2019 and (2) with all prevalent heart failure patients in 2021 who were vaccinated with either of the 2 mRNA vaccines (BNT162B2 and mRNA-1273).
The year 2019 was chosen as comparator because it was a year before the COVID-19 pandemic, and it was a year with an average risk of infection and death due to the influenza virus.
Patients who had heart failure for >10 years were excluded to ensure validity of the diagnosis code, along with patients under the age of 40 years and over the age of 95 years.
The patients in the 2 cohorts were matched using exact exposure matching on age, sex, and duration of heart failure (in intervals of 1 year).

The outcomes of interest included risk of 90-day all-cause mortality and risk of 90-day worsening heart failure defined as a readmission for heart failure (in-hospital admission lasting >24 hours), 90-day risk of venous thromboembolism (pulmonary embolism or deep venous thromboembolism), 90-day risk of myocarditis, and 90-day risk of pneumonia.
For patients in the 2021 (vaccinated) cohort, the index date was defined as the date of the patients’ second vaccination.
The second vaccination date was chosen because adverse events were expected to be the highest after the second vaccination.
Patients in the 2019 (unvaccinated) cohort were assigned the index day and month of their 1:1 match in the 2021 cohort but used the prevaccination index year 2019.

When analyzing the outcomes of worsening heart failure, myocarditis, and pulmonary embolism, patients were followed from index to 90 days, an outcome, death, or study end (September 30), whichever came first.
For the analyses of all-cause mortality, patients were followed for 90 days, death, or study end, whichever came first.

Comorbidities were identified using the _International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision_, diagnosis codes registered up to 10 years before the index date; atrial fibrillation, ischemic heart disease, acute myocardial infarction, stroke, peripheral vascular disease, cancer, chronic kidney disease, chronic obstructive lung disease, depression, gout, dementia, mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis, and hemodialysis.
Information on diabetes and hypertension was identified from the use of antidiabetic drugs and at least 2 types of antihypertensive medication, respectively (Tables S1 and S2).

Baseline pharmacotherapy was identified through the Danish National Prescription Registry and included the ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor, angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs), amiodarone, β-blockers, calcium channel blockers, vasodilators, digoxin, thiazide loop diuretics, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, statins, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, statins, oral anticoagulants, antiplatelets, SGLT2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter-2) inhibitors, and angiotensin II receptor neprilysin inhibitors.
Patients were defined as users if they had filled a prescription within 180 days before the index date (Table S2).
Categorical variables were summarized as counts with percentages and continuous variables as medians with interquartile ranges.

The Kaplan-Meier method was used to estimate crude absolute risk of all-cause mortality and the Aalen-Johansen method to estimate the absolute risk of worsening of heart failure, myocarditis, and venous thromboembolism.
Outcome-specific Cox regression analyses were performed for the hazard rates of all outcomes and also for the hazard rate of death without outcome (competing risk).

All Cox regression models were adjusted for vaccine status (2019 versus 2021) and additive effects of the following risk factors: duration of heart failure, sex, age (40–59, 60–79, and 80–95), current use of SGLT2 inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor neprilysin inhibitors, history of ischemic heart disease, cancer, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, and admission with heart failure <90 days before index.
Sensitivity analyses were performed additionally standardizing to ACE inhibitor/ARB, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and statins.

Based on the outcome-specific Cox regression and the Cox regression for the competing risk, we calculated 90-day outcome-specific absolute risks, that is, the predicted probability that the outcome occurs in the 90-day-long period after the index date using the formula that combines the hazard rates of the outcome with the hazard rates of the competing risk.14,15 For the all-cause mortality outcome, the predicted probabilities were obtained from the all-cause mortality Cox regression model.
Note that the predicted probabilities depend on the risk factors.

Standardized average 90-day outcome risks were calculated as average predicted probabilities evaluated at all observed patient risk factors in either cohort but setting the vaccine status.16 The standard population is the union of the 2019 and the 2021 cohorts.

We reported the average treatment effects as standardized differences in absolute 90-day outcome risks between setting vaccine status to vaccinated and setting it to nonvaccinated.15 Further analyses were performed to investigate the differences in the standardized 90-day risk differences across subgroups (age, sex, ischemic heart disease, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, admission with heart failure <90 days before index, current use of SGLT2 inhibitors, and angiotensin II receptor neprilysin inhibitors).

Noteworthy, within the limitations of the data and regression models, it is possible to interpret the standardized absolute risk differences as what would have occurred if the patients had been randomized to either take the vaccine or to not take it.
We used the reverse Kaplan-Meier method to estimate the percentage of censored patients.
The level of statistical significance was set at 5%.
Data management and statistical analysis were performed using the statistical software R.

Several sensitivity analyses were performed and included matching with the years of 2018 and 2017, to investigate the temporal trends in risk of all-cause mortality, worsening heart failure, venous thromboembolism, or myocarditis.

Pneumonia was chosen as an outcome because it could either be an indicator of an additional immunological effect by protecting against other viral respiratory infections or it could be a proxy for social distancing.
Additionally, any fractures were used as a negative outcome control, as the mRNA vaccines are believed not to influence the risk of this outcome.

Analyses on the risk of all-cause mortality, worsening heart failure, venous thromboembolism, or myocarditis in patients receiving at least 1 dosage (followed from the first dosage) and in patients aged 18 to 40 years were performed.

Additional supplementary analyses were performed investigating the risk of any of the outcome, including COVID-19 deaths and pneumonia in all prevalent heart failure patients in 2021 vaccinated and not vaccinated.
Patients not vaccinated were matched 1:1 using exact exposure matching on sex, age, and duration of heart failure and were followed from the date of the second vaccination.
Patients in the nonvaccinated cohort were assigned the index day and month of their 1:1 match in the vaccinated cohort.
Retrospective studies based on Danish registry data do not require ethical approval.
The data-responsible institution (Capital Region of Denmark) approved the study (approval number P-2019-191).
A total of 78 732 prevalent heart failure patients were identified on January 1, 2021.
Of the eligible patients for inclusion, 8.3% did not receive a vaccine, and of these, 42% died during the follow-up period (September 30, 2021).
For those patients who received a vaccine, 91.6% were vaccinated with BNT162B2 and 8.3% were vaccinated with mRNA-1273.
Less than 0.1% were vaccinated with ChAdOx1 and Ad26.COV2.S.
Table S3 shows the patient characteristics by vaccination status, and Figure S1 shows the time line for the first and second dosage in patients who received a vaccination.
Overall, patients who did not receive a vaccine had more comorbidity such as chronic kidney disease, chronic obstructive lung disease, and diabetes.
The total study population comprised 101 786 patients, with 50 893 patients in each cohort (Figure 1).
The median duration of heart failure was 4.1 (interquartile range, 2.0–6.7) years, and 13.8% were in the age groups 40 to 59 years, 55% in 60 to 79 years, and 31.1% in 80 to 95 years (Table).
Approximately 63% had no prior hospital admission with heart failure, whereas 3.0% (2021 cohort) and 3.4% (2019 cohort) had >2 prior hospital admissions with heart failure.

A higher number of patients in the 2019 (unvaccinated) cohort had ischemic heart disease, peripheral artery disease, chronic kidney disease, hypertension, chronic obstructive lung disease, or had been admitted with heart failure 90 days before the index date.

In contrast, a higher number of patients in the 2021 (vaccinated) cohort had prevalent cancer, diabetes, and used more concomitant medication, such as ACE/ARB, statins, and mineralocorticoid steroids.

A total number of 1113 patients died in the 2021 (vaccinated) cohort, and 1313 patients died in the 2019 (unvaccinated) cohort.

The standardized risk of all-cause mortality within 90 days was 2.22% (95% CI, 2.10%–2.36%) in the 2021 (vaccinated) cohort and 2.56% (95% CI, 2.42%–2.70%) in the 2019 (unvaccinated) cohort, showing a significant difference in the risk of all-cause mortality between the 2 cohorts (risk difference, −0.33% [95% CI, −0.52% to −0.15%]; Figures 2 and 3; Figure S2).

In patients without diabetes, the standardized risk was 2.33% (95% CI, 2.19%–2.48%) in the 2019 (unvaccinated) cohort and 2.17% (95% CI, 2.03%–2.31%) in the 2021 (vaccinated) cohort (risk difference, −0.16% [95% CI, −0.36%–0.04%]; Figure 4; Figure S3).

In patients with diabetes, the standardized risk was 3.17% (95% CI, 2.85%–3.48%) in the 2019 (unvaccinated) cohort and 2.40% (95% CI, 2.12%–2.66%) in the 2021 (vaccinated) cohort (risk difference, −0.76% [95% CI, −1.19% to −0.34%]).

In patients with a heart failure admission <90 days before index, the standardized risk was 12.01% (95% CI, 9.86%–14.16%) in the 2019 (unvaccinated) cohort and 8.98% (95% CI, 6.91%–11.05%) in the 2021 (vaccinated) cohort (risk difference, −3.03% [95% CI, −5.95% to −0.11%]).

The standardized risk of worsening heart failure within 90 days was 1.10% (95% CI, −1.01% to 1.19%) in the 2021 (vaccinated) cohort and 1.08% (95% CI, 0.99%–1.17%) in the 2019 (unvaccinated) cohort, showing no significant difference in the risk of worsening heart failure between the groups (risk difference, 0.02% [95% CI, −0.11% to 0.15%]; Figures 2 and 3).

In patients with a heart failure admission <90 days before index, the standardized risk was 13.23% (95% CI, 10.85%–15.61%) in the 2019 (unvaccinated) cohort and 11.32% (95% CI, 9.01%–13.63%) in the 2021 (vaccinated) cohort (risk difference, −1.91% [95% CI, −5.25% to 1.43%]; Figure 5; Figure S4).

Only 3 events of myocarditis were identified in the 2019 (unvaccinated) cohort and 7 events in the 2021 (vaccinated) cohort, showing no significant difference in the risk of myocarditis between the 2 groups.

The standardized risk of venous thromboembolism was 0.06% (95% CI, 0.04%–0.08%) in the 2021 (vaccinated) cohort and 0.08% (95% CI, 0.05%–0.10%) in the 2019 (unvaccinated) cohort, showing no significant difference in the risk of venous thromboembolism between the groups (risk difference, −0.02% [95% CI, −0.05% to 0.01%]; Figures 2 and 3).

The standardized risk of pneumonia was 1.38% (95% CI, 1.27%–1.48%) in the 2021 (vaccinated) cohort and 2.03% (95% CI, 1.91%–2.15%) in the 2019 (unvaccinated) cohort, showing a significant difference in the risk of pneumonia between the groups (risk difference, −0.64% [95% CI, −0.81% to −0.49%]; Figure S5).
Matching the 2021 cohort with a 2017 and 2018 cohort of prevalent heart failure patients showed similar results as the main analysis and for all other outcomes (Tables S4 and S5; Figures S6 and S7).
Additionally, there was no significant difference in the risk of any fractures between the 2 groups (Figure S8).
Similar results were found when analyzing the risk of all-cause mortality, worsening heart failure, venous thromboembolism, or myocarditis after receiving 1 dosage (Figure S9).
Among 813 patients with heart failure aged 18 to 40 years, similar results were found regarding the risk of all-cause mortality and risk of worsening heart failure (Table S6; Figure S10).
No events for myocarditis or venous thromboembolism were found in this age group.

When performing supplementary analyses on prevalent heart failure patients in 2021 vaccinated and not vaccinated, matched on sex, age, and duration of heart failure (3830 patients in each cohort; Table S7; Figures S11 through S13), it was observed that those patients not vaccinated were at a higher risk of all-cause mortality and also higher risk of worsening heart failure.

Unvaccinated patients also had a higher risk of dying from SARS COVID-19 (risk difference, −1.40% [95% CI, −1.85% to −1.03%]) and higher risk of pneumonia (risk difference, −2.17% [95% CI, −2.89% to −1.46%]).
Additional analyses including ACE inhibitor/ARB, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and statins in the main analyses showed similar results as the main analysis (Figure S14).

Supplementary analyses showed that due to administrative censoring on September 30, 8.01% of the unvaccinated and 8.04% of the vaccinated patients were not observed for the full period of 90 days (Figure S15).
In this nationwide register-based study, we investigated the safety of the 2 mRNA vaccines BNT162B2 and mRNA-1273 in patients with heart failure.

The main findings of this study were (1) receiving an mRNA vaccination was safe and even associated with a slightly reduced risk of mortality and pneumonia compared with not being vaccinated; (2) receiving an mRNA vaccination was not associated with an increased risk of worsening heart failure; and (3) receiving an mRNA vaccination was not associated with a detectable increase in the risk of either myocarditis or venous thromboembolism.

Little is known about the impact of the mRNA COVID vaccines in patients with heart failure, despite the fact that COVID vaccination is highly recommended in these patients, due to the patients’ high risk of morbidity and mortality from SARS-CoV-2.1 In this study, we were able to investigate the safety of the mRNA vaccines in a real-world heart failure patient population and found no safety concerns, consistent with the overall findings in the large, randomized trials that have investigated the safety and efficacy of the mRNA vaccines.2,4,5 It has been recommended that patients with heart failure should be vaccinated when they are in a stable clinical condition.

However, this statement was not supported by current evidence.1 Our results showed that the mRNA vaccine was safe in patients with recently decompensated heart failure (ie, who were admitted with heart failure 90 days before index) and in patients with concomitant type 2 diabetes.
Therefore, our data suggest that high-risk heart failure patients can safely receive mRNA vaccination for COVID-19.
Although the study did not investigate the safety in patients with acutely decompensated heart failure, which may have had a different risk profile.
In addition, we were able to show that receiving a vaccination had no impact on the patients’ risk of worsening heart failure.
Concerns have been raised regarding an increased risk of myocarditis, after vaccination with the mRNA vaccines.
The reported cases have been few and have mainly occurred in young men.
A recent study by Husby et al 17 found a significantly increased risk of myocarditis mainly driven by men and adolescents/adults aged 12 to 39 years.
Likewise, a study by Mevorach et al 18 also found a higher incidence of myocarditis in adolescents who received BNT162b2.
In this study, where we excluded patients under the age of 40 years and thereby also adolescents, no significantly increased risk of myocarditis was found.
However, when performing sensitivity analyses for patients aged 18 to 40 years, no increased risk of myocarditis was found, likely explained by the low number of patients in this age group.

Myocarditis is a rare event following mRNA vaccination, occurring in 20 to 30 per million vaccinated.19 Another safety concern regarding the COVID vaccines was raised after cases of venous thromboembolism and severe hemorrhage, later identified as the syndrome vaccine-induced thrombocytopenia.20 However, these concerns were mainly raised with the 2 viral vector vaccines ChAdOx1 and Ad26.COV2.S and not with the mRNA vaccines, and results from this study suggest no increased risk of venous thromboembolism associated with the mRNA vaccines in patients with HF.

Pharmacological and nonpharmacological therapies have significantly improved the prognosis for patients with heart failure, which includes ACE/ARB, SGLT2 inhibitors, and angiotensin II receptor neprilysin inhibitors.31,32 Evidence suggests that patients with heart failure have a persistent immune activation, and studies have shown that these patients have increased plasma and serum levels of inflammatory cytokines including TNF-α (tumor necrosis factor alpha) and interleukins 1 and 6.33 Several trials, including the ACCLAIM trial (Advanced Chronic Heart Failure Clinical Assessment of Immune Modulation Therapy [immunological]),34 the GISII-HF trial (Effect of Rosuvastatin in Patients With Chronic Heart Failure [anti-inflammatory]),35 and the RENEWAL trial (Randomized Etanercept Worldwide Evaluation; immunological),36 have investigated immunomodulation in heart failure patients showing no effect of immunomodulation.

However, it would be interesting to conduct further studies that focus on the nonspecific modulation of the immune response in patients with heart failure, to investigate whether there will be a clinical benefit.
Several strengths apply to this study.
First, we were able to include the whole patient population included in a nationwide vaccination program, and we have information on all vaccinations that were administered.
In addition, we had complete follow-up on all patients included in the study.
However, some limitations also apply to this study.

It is possible that we have excluded sick and potentially terminal heart failure patients from the 2021 cohort, as those were probably more likely not to receive a vaccination, while those potentially sick patients were not excluded in the 2019 cohort.

Despite an effort to adjust for the differences in patient characteristics between the 2 cohorts, we might have introduced healthy vaccine bias, which may have led to an overestimation of the effect of the vaccine.37 Another limitation is the lack of important information on certain clinical variables such as left ventricular ejection fraction, renal function, NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide), and New York Heart Association class (unmeasured confounding).
However, it should be noted that we did not observe an early separation of the curves for the cumulative risk indicating that we did introduce excessive selection bias.
This study found that the SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination was not associated with an increased risk of worsening heart failure, myocarditis, venous thromboembolism, or all-cause mortality.
This suggests there should be no concern regarding the use of the mRNA vaccine in patients with heart failure in relation to the risk of cardiovascular side effects.
